record.paper_title: Models, feedback control, and open problems of 3D bipedal robotic walking
record.original_question: Compute or characterize the domain of attraction of a periodic walking gait for a bipedal robot, especially in the hybrid-systems setting and in the presence of modeling errors that arise when transferring a controller from simulation to the physical robot. The problem asks for practical ways to estimate which perturbations and initial conditions still converge to the desired periodic gait.

evidence.quote: What remains an almost completely unexplored area is computing the domain of attraction for periodic solutions, even for dynamical systems.

Characterizing the domain of attraction of a periodic walking gait for a bipedal robot model is an important consideration with respect to the eventual implementation of the corresponding feedback controller on the actual biped.
There will naturally be errors in the model of the biped, and accounting for these while estimating the domain of attraction would be very useful when passing from simulation to experimentation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a planar or three-dimensional bipedal walking robot modeled as a hybrid dynamical system: continuous-time rigid-body Lagrangian dynamics during the single- (and possibly double-) support phase, together with a discrete reset map modeling the instantaneous impact of the swing leg with the ground. Let the closed-loop system, under a chosen feedback controller, admit an exponentially stable periodic orbit O (a hybrid limit cycle) corresponding to a desired walking gait, with associated Poincaré return map P having a fixed point x* whose linearization is Schur stable.

(1) Develop a constructive method to compute or rigorously inner-approximate the domain of attraction D(O) := { x in the hybrid state space : the trajectory starting at x is defined for all forward time and converges to O } of such a hybrid periodic orbit, going beyond local linearization at x*.

(2) Extend the method to the robust setting: given a family of admissible perturbations to the continuous and discrete dynamics (e.g., bounded parametric model errors in inertia, mass, link lengths, contact location, and impact map), characterize or inner-approximate the robust domain of attraction—the set of initial conditions guaranteed to converge to a neighborhood of the nominal gait for every admissible perturbation—so that the estimate yields practical guarantees when transferring a controller designed in simulation to the physical robot.

Provide either an algorithmic procedure (with convergence/soundness guarantees) or analytic characterizations producing certified inner approximations of D(O), together with quantitative bounds in terms of the size of the modeling errors.
artifact.category_tag: Domain of attraction for hybrid periodic orbits
artifact.status_search_result: Computation of regions of attraction for hybrid limit cycles in bipedal walking remains an active research area. Recent works (e.g., SOS/Lyapunov-based RoA computation for hybrid limit cycles, cell-mapping methods, and contraction-based estimates) provide partial inner approximations and locally certified results, but a general, scalable, and robust characterization that accounts for modeling errors when transferring controllers from simulation to hardware is still considered open. No definitive solution to the general problem has been reported.

status_evidence.title: Computation of Regions of Attraction for Hybrid Limit Cycles
status_evidence.snippet: Region-of-attraction (RoA) for a walking gait represents robot configurations from which it can eventually converge to the corresponding hybrid limit cycle.
status_evidence.claim: RoA computation for hybrid limit cycles is an active and only partially solved research topic.

status_evidence.title: Stable Walking of a Biped Robot (cell mapping)
status_evidence.snippet: The periodic domain of attraction is solved using the cell mapping method.
status_evidence.claim: Partial numerical methods (cell mapping) exist for estimating the periodic domain of attraction.
